subject: Science
source: National Curriculum KS1 Science (Living things and their habitats); Drive Science folder 'Science lower school' (3.8 organisms, 3.9 eco-systems)

lessons.title: Living, dead and never alive
objectives: Sort things into living, dead and never been alive
Use the seven life processes in simple words
Explain why a thing is living or not

keywords.def: alive now: it moves, feeds, grows and reproduces
once alive but no longer alive
something that has never been alive, like a rock
to have young or make new plants

starter: Bismillah. Name one living thing in a garden.
Name one thing that is not alive.
What do animals and plants need to stay alive?

teach.heading: What does living mean?
teach.note: Teach the life processes in child-friendly words: move, breathe, feed, grow, reproduce, sense, get rid of waste. Plants move by growing and turning towards light. Do not overload; use three at first.

teach.heading: Dead things
teach.note: Show a dry leaf, a feather, a piece of wood. They were once alive. Misconception: a fallen leaf is a living thing; explain it is dead.

teach.heading: Things never alive
bullets: A toy car is not living
teach.note: A pencil is made from wood but is made into an object; keep simple: it is not alive. Ask 'Does a rock need food?'

teach.heading: Sorting game
teach.note: Safe online activity: children bring three household objects (spoon, leaf, toy) and sort into three groups. Check each decision with the question 'Does it need food and water?'

practice: Is a dandelion living, dead or never alive?
Is a stone living, dead or never alive? Explain.
A wooden table was made from a tree. Is the table living, dead or never alive?
independent: Draw a three-column table: living, dead, never alive. Put five things in the columns.
Write one sentence: 'A cat is living because ...'
exit: Give an example of a living thing.
Is a pebble living, dead or never alive?
lessons.homework: Find three things in your home that are living, dead or never alive. Draw them and label them.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use picture cards for sorting and sentence starters 'It is ... because ...'. Stretch: explain why a seed is living even though it does not seem to move.

lessons.title: Habitats
objectives: Match animals and plants to their habitats
Explain why a habitat suits the living things in it

keywords.def: the place where a plant or animal lives
the surroundings of a living thing
a place that keeps an animal safe or protected
a very dry habitat with little water

starter: Bismillah. Is a spider living, dead or never alive?
Where does a fish live? Where does a bird live?
What do all living things need?

teach.heading: What is a habitat?
teach.note: Habitat = natural home of a plant or animal. Ask 'Where do you live?' then 'Where does a fox live?'

teach.heading: Different habitats
teach.note: Show photos of ocean, woodland, desert and pond. Link to camels in desert (children may know camels from family countries). Ask what makes each habitat different (water, shade, temperature).

teach.heading: Why the match works
bullets: A camel stores fat in its hump
A fish has gills and fins
A polar bear has thick fur
teach.note: Camel humps store fat, not water: a common misconception. Explain that the animal's body helps it live in its habitat.

teach.heading: Looking after habitats
bullets: Allah made us carers of the Earth
teach.note: Keep Islamic ethos natural: we are trusted to look after Allah's creation. Ask 'What can you do?' (put litter in a bin, save water).

practice: Which habitat is best for a fish: a pond or a desert?
Why does a camel live well in the desert?
Match: owl, crab, lizard. Habitats: woodland, seashore, desert.
independent: Draw one habitat and two living things that live there. Label them.
Write: 'A ... lives in a ... because it has ...'
exit: Name one animal and the habitat it lives in.
lessons.homework: Choose one animal. Find out where it lives and draw its habitat.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a habitat picture matching sheet with key words. Stretch: explain why a polar bear could not live in the desert.

lessons.title: Microhabitats
objectives: Name small animals that live in microhabitats
Explain why they choose damp, dark places

keywords.def: a very small habitat, like under a stone
a small animal such as a worm, snail or woodlouse
looking carefully to see and count what is there

starter: Name a habitat and an animal that lives in it.
What do living things need from their habitat?

teach.heading: Tiny habitats
bullets: Under a log is a microhabitat
teach.note: Show photos of a log pile and a leaf litter. The smaller the home, the smaller the animals.

teach.heading: Minibeasts
teach.note: Show photos. Why damp? Woodlice breathe through gill-like structures and dry out. Keep language simple: 'they like it damp and dark'.

teach.heading: Safe minibeast hunt
teach.note: Safe online practical: children with a grown-up look under a flowerpot or log in a garden, or you show a short video of a minibeast hunt. Look only; never pick up animals. Wash hands with soap after. Cleanliness is part of faith (hadith in Sahih Muslim: cleanliness is half of faith).

teach.heading: Recording what we find
teach.note: Model a tally chart with 5-bar gates for snails, worms, woodlice. Practise tallying to 8 together.

practice: Where might you find a woodlouse: under a stone or on a sunny wall?
Why do small animals like damp places?
independent: Draw a tally chart for woodlice (4), snails (3), worms (5) and fill it in.
Draw a microhabitat under a log and label two animals.
lessons.homework: With a grown-up, look carefully in a garden or park for a microhabitat. Draw one minibeast you see. Wash your hands.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a picture tally sheet. Stretch: compare two microhabitats and say which has more minibeasts and why.

lessons.title: Simple food chains
objectives: Say that all animals need food
Build and explain a simple food chain with arrows

keywords.def: a line showing what eats what
a plant that makes its own food
an animal that hunts and eats other animals
an animal that is hunted and eaten

starter: Name a minibeast and its home.
Where do animals get their food from?

teach.heading: Where food comes from
teach.note: Ask 'Who eats grass?' (rabbit, cow). Say 'plants use sunlight to make their own food' without detail. Energy begins with the Sun.

teach.heading: A food chain
teach.note: Draw: grass -> rabbit -> fox. Read it aloud: 'The grass is eaten by the rabbit.' Misconception: arrows mean 'goes to'. Stress 'is eaten by'.

teach.heading: Predator and prey
bullets: Prey can be a plant eater
teach.note: Predator hunts; prey is hunted. Many animals can be both: a small bird eats insects and is eaten by a hawk.

teach.heading: Pond chain
teach.note: Model another chain so children see the pattern: plant first. Ask children to suggest the last link.

practice: Which one is the predator: rabbit or fox?
Read this chain aloud: leaf -> caterpillar -> bird.
independent: Draw a food chain with three living things and arrows. Label the producer.
Write two sentences about your chain using 'is eaten by'.
exit: What does the arrow in a food chain mean?
lessons.homework: Make a food chain for a garden using three animals or plants you know. Draw and label it.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use cut-out pictures to arrange the chain. Stretch: build a four-link chain and name the predator and prey.
